steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on constrained bimanual motion planning using analytic inverse kinematics. Motivate why two-arm tasks matter and why the task-space constraints are hard, review general constrained-planning techniques, introduce our idea of parametrizing the constraint manifold with analytic IK, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Bimanual robots need to be able to execute coordinated actions with both arms in order to reach (super)human-like skill in automation and home contexts. There are many tasks that can only be solved when two arms manipulate together, such as carrying an unwieldy object, folding clothes, or assembling parts. In many manipulation tasks one gripper can be used to fixture the manipuland while the other one does the desired action; examples are opening a bottle, chopping vegetables, and tightening a bolt. Also, some tools explicitly need two arms to use, like hand mixers, rolling pins, and can openers.

For many of these tasks, the motion of the robot arms is subject to equality constraints imposed in task space. For example, when an object is held by both hands and moved, the robot has to make sure that the transformation between the end effectors stays constant. In configuration space these task space constraints show up as complicated nonlinear equality constraints, and this is a major challenge for traditional motion planning algorithms.

The existing literature has general techniques for handling task-space constraints in configuration-space planning. Sampling-based planners can project samples onto the constraint manifold or use numerical continuation to build piecewise-linear approximations. Constraints can also be relaxed or enforced directly with trajectory optimization. For some bimanual planning problems there is extra structure that these general methods do not exploit. For certain classes of robot arms, analytic inverse kinematics (analytic IK) can map an end-effector pose (along with additional parameters to resolve kinematic redundancy) to joint angles in closed form. These solutions are specific to certain classes of robot arms, but they are a powerful tool to use if they are available. Luckily, analytic IK is available for many popular robot arms today, including the KUKA iiwa. See Figure 1.

- Our approach
  - plan for "controllable" arm; "subordinate" arm follows via analytic IK mapping
  - configurations where subordinate can't reach or violates joint limits = obstacles
  - parametrize constraint manifold -> feasible set has positive measure in new planning space
  - no equality constraints -> sampling-based planners unmodified
  - differentiate through IK -> trajectory optimization directly
- Organization
  - overview of constrained motion planning techniques + available analytic IK solutions
  - our parametrization; geometric and topological properties
  - slight modifications to standard planners (sampling-based, trajectory optimization)
  - convex sets in new configuration space, collision free + kinematically valid; needed for Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)
  - experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bimanual robots need to be able to execute coordinated actions with both arms in order to reach (super)human-like skill in automation and home contexts. There are many tasks that can only be solved when two arms manipulate together, such as carrying an unwieldy object, folding clothes, or assembling parts. In many manipulation tasks one gripper can be used to fixture the manipuland while the other one does the desired action; examples are opening a bottle, chopping vegetables, and tightening a bolt. Also, some tools explicitly need two arms to use, like hand mixers, rolling pins, and can openers.

For many of these tasks, the motion of the robot arms is subject to equality constraints imposed in task space. For example, when an object is held by both hands and moved, the robot has to make sure that the transformation between the end effectors stays constant. In configuration space these task space constraints show up as complicated nonlinear equality constraints, and this is a major challenge for traditional motion planning algorithms.

The existing literature has general techniques for handling task-space constraints in configuration-space planning. Sampling-based planners can project samples onto the constraint manifold or use numerical continuation to build piecewise-linear approximations. Constraints can also be relaxed or enforced directly with trajectory optimization. For some bimanual planning problems there is extra structure that these general methods do not exploit. For certain classes of robot arms, analytic inverse kinematics (analytic IK) can map an end-effector pose (along with additional parameters to resolve kinematic redundancy) to joint angles in closed form. These solutions are specific to certain classes of robot arms, but they are a powerful tool to use if they are available. Luckily, analytic IK is available for many popular robot arms today, including the KUKA iiwa. See Figure 1.

When a robot has to move an object that it is holding with both hands, we propose to construct a plan for one "controllable" arm, and then make the other "subordinate" arm follow it through an analytic IK mapping. Configurations where the subordinate arm cannot reach the end-effector of the primary arm, or where reaching it would violate joint limits, are treated as obstacles. This way we parametrize the constraint manifold so that the feasible set has positive measure in the new planning space. Since we don't have to consider the equality constraints anymore, sampling-based planning algorithms can be used without modification. We can also differentiate through the IK mapping, so trajectory optimization approaches can be applied directly.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. First, we give an overview of the existing techniques for constrained motion planning and describe the available analytic IK solutions. Then we present our parametrization of the constraint manifold for bimanual planning and discuss its relevant geometric and topological properties. We describe the slight modifications needed to adapt standard planning algorithms (including sampling-based planning and trajectory optimization) to work in this framework. Then we present a technique for generating convex sets in this new configuration space, such that every configuration within such a set is collision free and kinematically valid. These sets are essential for planning frameworks such as Graph of Convex Sets (GCS). Finally, we present various experiments that demonstrate the efficacy of these new techniques.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Enabling bimanual robots to execute coordinated actions with both arms is essential for achieving (super)human-like skill in automation and home contexts. There exists a variety of tasks that are only solvable when two arms manipulate in concert [1], such as carrying an unwieldy object, folding clothes, or assembling parts. In many manipulation tasks, one gripper can be used to provide fixture to the manipuland while the other performs the desired action [2]; such tasks include opening a bottle, chopping vegetables, and tightening a bolt. Furthermore, some tools explicitly require two arms to use, such as hand mixers, rolling pins, and can openers.

To accomplish many of these tasks, the motion of the robot arms becomes subject to equality constraints imposed in task space. For example, when moving an object that is held by both hands, the robot must ensure that the transformation between the end effectors remains constant. Such task space constraints appear as complicated nonlinear equality constraints in configuration space, posing a major challenge to traditional motion planning algorithms.

In the existing literature, there are general techniques for handling task-space constraints in configuration-space planning. Sampling-based planners can project samples onto the constraint manifold [3] or use numerical continuation [4] to construct piecewise-linear approximations. Constraints can also be relaxed [5] or enforced directly with trajectory optimization [6]. For certain bimanual planning problems, however, there is additional structure that these general methods do not exploit. For certain classes of robot arms, analytic inverse kinematics (analytic IK) can be used to map an end-effector pose (along with additional parameters to resolve kinematic redundancy) to joint angles in closed form. Such solutions are specific to certain classes of robot arms, but are a powerful tool to be leveraged if available. Fortunately, analytic IK is available for many popular robot arms today, including the KUKA iiwa. See Figure 1.

If a robot must move an object that it is holding with both hands, we propose constructing a plan for one "controllable" arm, and then the other "subordinate" arm can be made to follow it via an analytic IK mapping. Configurations where the subordinate arm cannot reach the end-effector of the primary arm, or where doing so would require violating joint limits, are treated as obstacles. In this way, we parametrize the constraint manifold so that the feasible set has positive measure in the new planning space. Because we no longer have to consider the equality constraints, sampling-based planning algorithms can be applied without modification. We can also differentiate through the IK mapping, enabling the direct application of trajectory optimization approaches.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. First, we give an overview of the existing techniques used for constrained motion planning and describe the available analytic IK solutions. Then, we present our parametrization of the constraint manifold for bimanual planning and discuss its relevant geometric and topological properties. We describe the slight modifications necessary to adapt standard planning algorithms (including sampling-based planning and trajectory optimization) to operate in this framework. We then present a technique for generating convex sets in this new configuration space, such that every configuration within such a set is collision free and kinematically valid. These sets are essential for planning frameworks such as Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) [7,8]. Finally, we present various experiments demonstrating the efficacy of these new techniques.

References:
[1] F. Krebs and T. Asfour, “A bimanual manipulation taxonomy,” IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters , vol. 7, no. 4, pp. 11 031–11 038, 2022.
[2] R. Holladay, T. Lozano-Pérez, and A. Rodriguez, “Robust planning for multi-stage forceful manipulation,” The International Journal of Robotics Research , vol. 43, no. 3, pp. 330–353, 2024. [Online]. Available: https://doi.org/10.1177/02783649231198560
